extracted.intended_audience: researchers preparing NIH-style grant Specific Aims pages (PIs, postdocs, graduate students, research staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and template for drafting the one-page Specific Aims section of an NIH-style grant application: how to structure the preamble, write 2–4 Specific Aims, and craft the payoff paragraph so reviewers understand significance, innovation, approach, investigator, and environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe how proposed work fills a gap in knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Your Aims page describes how your proposed work will fill an gap in knowledge that is preventing the field from moving forward; it summarizes the general research steps by which you will test your hypotheses; and it gives the reviewer confidence that you are the team that can accomplish the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the single gap clearly in the Preamble (see 'GAP in knowledge' below). Explain how filling that gap will advance the field and why the proposed approach addresses the gap rather than merely describing the missing thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on an important problem / significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on an important problem, unresolved issue, barrier to advancing the field, or gap in knowledge. The answers you seek must be important to the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the significance of your research to science and health in the payoff and elsewhere. Make clear why reviewers and the broader community should care about the outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims are narrowly focused, concrete, and achievable
rubrics_metrics.description: Aims are narrowly focused, concrete objectives you can achieve during the grant; Aims are your short-term objectives/project milestones — not your long-term research goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose 2–4 Aims depending on grant and project length. Ask how much work you can realistically accomplish in the requested time. Ensure each Aim is time-bound and attainable within the grant period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit hypothesis and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state your hypothesis and why testing it is important. The overall hypothesis should flow from your preliminary data/unique assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State an overall central hypothesis in the Preamble and per-Aim hypotheses where appropriate. Explain why you formed the hypothesis (prelim data, literature) and how testing it will advance knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments must test the hypothesis (testability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The experiments you propose must be able to test your hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly describe methods or experimental steps that will provide the expected readouts; ensure outcomes/readouts are measurable so reviewers can judge whether the Aim will answer the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual Aims are logically related but not dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual Aims are not inter-dependent but are supportive of each other. They flow logically, but can’t be absolutely dependent on a particular outcome of another Aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design Aims so failing one Aim does not completely derail the others. Describe logical links but avoid serial dependency that could threaten overall success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touch on NIH review criteria (SIAIE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be able to get a good sense of review criteria (Significance, Innovation, Approach, Investigator, Environment) from the Aims page. Make sure you touch on all five.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include brief cues about innovation and feasibility, note investigator qualifications and institutional resources, and clearly state significance and approach so reviewers can map the Aims to scoring criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and level of explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aims page is targeted at primary and secondary reviewers, other study group members, program staff and advisory board and council members. Write Aims for less of an expert compared to the rest of the application (~level of 'Scientific American').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t assume deep expertise in your specific subfield; write for both experts and smart general scientists. Learn your study section rosters and tailor framing to likely reviewer expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and equivalence of Aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of each Aim as one paper, or a significant part of a paper. Each Aim should take about the same amount of time/effort and be of about equal importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid one overly large Aim and two minor ones; aim for roughly balanced scope so reviewers perceive a coherent, achievable project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not propose too much / realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself how much work can you realistically accomplish in the time you are requesting. Aims are short-term objectives not long-term goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit scope to what can be done in the grant period; proposing too many ambitious Aims reduces credibility. Use the SMARTL criteria (see entry) to check realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: SMARTL criteria for Aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Aims can be tested against the 'SMARTL' criteria: Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, Time-bound, Learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific — include why/who/what/how/where/when/which/how much; Measurable — can be tested empirically; Attainable — you and colleagues have expertise/resources; Relevant — field cares and it fits you; Time-bound — do-able within grant period; Learning — field and you learn something non-trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong actionable verbs; avoid vague descriptive verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin Aims with strong verbs (Apply, Test, Determine, Investigate, Characterize, Quantify, etc.) and avoid opening verbs that are too descriptive (Correlate, Describe, Understand, Develop, Examine, Measure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting an Aim with an active verb clarifies what you will do. Consider the 'To xxx' + action option to lead with the 'why' then 'what'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble: state big picture and central challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with BIG PICTURE — state the shared, central challenge of your field that lots of people are interested in solving (1–2 sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw the reader’s interest; avoid restating generic statistics. Frame the problem in terms meaningful to reviewers and funders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble: summarize knowns and set scene
rubrics_metrics.description: KNOWNS — elaborate on what is known about the central challenge and what has been going on to solve it (2–3 sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to set up the gap and show how your work fits into prior efforts; be concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble: name the single GAP in knowledge (the problem you will fill)
rubrics_metrics.description: The GAP in knowledge – Name a general gap in your field that is slowing or stopping progress towards achieving the big picture named in the first item. THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT: You must know which single gap your proposed work will fill; to fill this gap is WHY you are proposing this work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The GAP is seldom the lack of the thing you are proposing; rather, state the need in the field and how your idea addresses it. Try starting with 'however' or 'unfortunately.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble: elaborate on the gap and failed approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: ELABORATION on the gap — tell what you and others have tried or are trying and maybe why those approaches have not worked; tell how the gap prevents the field from advancing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly explain limitations of prior work and how those limitations sustain the gap, motivating your approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble: theory and uniqueness that motivates solution
rubrics_metrics.description: THEORY and UNIQUENESS — tell what unique thing(s) you know or have (e.g., preliminary findings or new data) and how that unique thing forms the basis for your thinking about how things work or what you are able to do to fill the gap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight preliminary data, novel resources, or methodological strengths that justify feasibility and novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble: state overall hypothesis and approach
rubrics_metrics.description: HYPOTHESIS — State the overall hypothesis that your Aims will test. YOUR APPROACH as the solution — State how you propose to fill the gap; state this in general terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis must flow from your unique data/qualifications. Keep approach high-level here; details belong in Approach section of full application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble: state why your team is right
rubrics_metrics.description: Your TEAM — If it is not already clear, tell why you are the right people to conduct the proposed research (1–2 sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly note key expertise, track record, and resources that make your team capable of accomplishing the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Aim components
rubrics_metrics.description: For each Specific Aim include: statement of the Aim (bold/underlined), any background not in the Preamble, why you are doing this Aim, hypothesis for this Aim, steps/some specifics/some techniques, and expected outcomes/readouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two suggested formats: (1) Start with a verb and what you'll do, then rationale/hypothesis/methods/expected outcomes; (2) Start with 'To xxx' (the WHY), then verb + what you'll do. Use sub-aim bullets for discrete steps if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub-aims presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sub-Aims are the smaller steps you plan to do to achieve an Aim. Consider presenting them as bullets if a few discrete steps are needed to achieve the Aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not using bullets, denote sequence with 'first, second, third' or 'first, then, next, finally'. Use numbering like 1A, 1B for clarity when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payoff paragraph (summary of significance/impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Payoff Paragraph states what successful completion of this work will 'buy' the field and the broader community: direct outputs (benefits), broader implications (value), and longer-term possibilities (potential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include expected direct outcomes for each Aim, explain why the work is innovative and what unique advantages you use, and describe impact beyond narrow interpretation and longer-term potential. Tie to funder priorities when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing style: clarity and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short, declarative sentences. Bullets are fine as appropriate. Be careful with opening verbs that could be interpreted as too descriptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the Aims aloud, redraft, and simplify. Ensure the page can be read quickly and gives reviewers a clear story and confidence in feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims check-up and feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Set your Aims draft aside, read it aloud, redraft, and get colleagues/mentors to read starting ~2 months before due date. Make sure reviewers are convinced the project is important and you can do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Imagine the papers you will write — would anyone be interested? Would the results be believed? Ensure the Aims page addressed all review criteria and that readers can identify your innovative contribution.
